name: Orthopathy

lead: Orthopathy is a health philosophy developed by the American physician Isaac Jennings in the 19th century. It holds that the body heals itself when it is rested and kept free of harmful habits, so adherents avoid drugs and favour a plain vegetarian diet, exercise, fresh air, sleep and, in the later natural hygiene movement, fasting. Its appeal to appearance-minded people is the chain of cleaner living, then better health, then clearer skin, steadier weight and more energy.

Its ideas were recorded in Jennings' 1867 book The Tree of Life and passed to natural hygiene writers such as Russell Trall and Herbert Shelton. It was a philosophical system rather than a tested protocol, and its claims have mostly been judged by historians and physicians rather than by trials.

paras: In practice the approach is a lifestyle: whole plant-based food, regular exercise, daylight and fresh air, bathing, good sleep and avoidance of alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea and spices, which Jennings opposed. Later natural hygienists added supervised or self-directed fasting. Results are described in terms of general vitality over months and years rather than a quick change.

Medical critics, then and now, object to the doctrine of avoiding drug treatment for illness, since serious conditions can go untreated. Fasting carries its own medical risks, particularly for people with existing conditions, and is generally discussed with a clinician. A nineteenth-century journal reviewer described Jennings' placebo-based methods as quackery.

angle.text: Followers treat healthy-looking skin and body composition as outcomes of living in line with natural laws. The route is lifestyle change rather than products or procedures, and benefits are described as gradual.

lead: Orthopathy is a 19th-century alternative-medicine philosophy developed by the American physician Isaac Jennings (1788-1874). The name comes from Greek roots meaning roughly "right affection", and Jennings set out the idea in his 1867 book The Tree of Life [1][2]. Its central claim is that illness is the body's own corrective process, and that the right response is to remove harmful habits and allow rest rather than to give drugs, an approach he called the "do-nothing cure" [2][2].

For people interested in how they look, orthopathy matters mostly as the root of natural hygiene, a tradition in which clean food, sleep, sunlight, exercise and fasting are credited with clearer skin, leaner bodies and a more vital appearance. Followers describe appearance as a by-product of health. The system recommends a vegetarian diet, bathing, rest and avoidance of alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea and spices [2][2].

Jennings' ideas drew on vitalism. Contemporary physicians criticised them; an 1867 review in the Buffalo Medical and Surgical Journal called his bread-pill methods quackery [2]. No clinical trials of orthopathy as a system exist; historians have studied how related hygiene teaching spread, for example in nineteenth-century Peru [3].

paras: Jennings practised conventional medicine, then grew disillusioned. According to biographical accounts, in 1822 he began giving patients placebos such as bread pills and coloured water, saw them improve, and concluded that drugs were unnecessary; he later stopped even placebos [2]. He lived in Oberlin, Ohio, where he served as a college trustee and wrote Medical Reform in 1847 [2].
In The Tree of Life (1867) he named his system orthopathy [1][2]. Later writers including Russell T. Trall, Felix Oswald and Herbert Shelton carried the ideas into the natural hygiene movement [2].

Orthopathy holds that the body possesses innate self-regulating and self-healing abilities, and that disease reflects violations of natural law such as overeating, poor air or stimulants [1]. Concepts associated with the broader hygiene tradition include enervation (nerve exhaustion) and toxemia (waste accumulation), treated with rest, hydrotherapy and fasting [1]. A vegetarian diet, bathing and rest were recommended, and Jennings opposed alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea, meat and spices [2].

Medical contemporaries were sceptical. An 1867 journal article called Jennings' bread-pill methods "down right quackery and imposition", and a review of The Tree of Life judged it without merit [2]. Summaries note that the system rests on anecdotal reports rather than controlled validation [1].

No studies found. Historical scholarship exists on hygiene education influenced by related European and Latin American traditions, for example a 2017 article on Sebastian Lorente's Catechism of Hygiene in Peru [3].
